papers.title: Do Machines Learn Deviance From Their Peers? A Randomized Test of Differential Association With AI Agents
papers.abstract: Differential association theory and its extension, social learning theory, hold that rule-breaking, and the definitions that make it acceptable, are learned through interaction with others. Because people choose their friends, this claim has been hard to test. We addressed this selection problem with AI agents, which learn only through communication and can be assigned to peers at random. In a preregistered experiment, 420 teams of three agents (1,260 agents; seven AI models) worked on coding tasks that could not be solved honestly. A scripted teammate said that it had cheated (deviant peer), that it had reported the problem honestly (honest peer), or said nothing (silent peer). Half of the teams were told that an auditor read their chat. Compared with a silent peer, a deviant peer increased cheating (66.2% vs. 62.9%; OR = 1.96) and an honest peer reduced it (55.7%; OR = 0.35). Among agents that cheated, a deviant peer increased claims that cheating was normal (13.7% vs. 3.4%), often as the team's norm. Monitoring did not suppress prohibited discussion; it doubled it. Peers mattered only for models that had not yet decided. AI agents offer a new way to test criminological learning theories without selection effects.
papers.topic_reason: Randomized experiment on peer influence and norm spread across 1,260 interacting AI agents in teams.
papers.one_sentence: Runs a preregistered experiment with 420 three-agent teams across seven AI models to test differential association theory. papers.title: Disenfranchisement in Spatial Voting Games
papers.abstract: The questions of voting rights, group membership, and the boundaries of acceptable discourse all involve a recursive, self-stability issue, wherein the voters, group members, and acceptable commentators are often the ultimate arbiters of their own rules for inclusion and exclusion. In order to understand how ideological or issue diversity may impact the stability of such inclusion and exclusion, we introduce franchise elections, where voting members of a group vote to change the electorate. In particular, when agents are positioned inside an ideological or issue space, a social choice function that aggregates agent viewpoints induces a preference for agents over group composition, where agents prefer groups that improve the social choice function outcome for them. We demonstrate that when ideological space is two-dimensional, these franchise elections can generate complex behavior and that this complexity exists for any social choice function. Using the Yolk social choice function from voting theory, we illustrate that franchise elections can predict that agents attempting to introduce a new ideological axis perpendicular to an existing left-right spectrum risk disenfranchisement unless they ally with either side of the spectrum, and that franchise elections can cycle with any period.
papers.topic_reason: Studies emergent, cyclic dynamics of group membership and voting rules across populations of agents.
papers.one_sentence: Introduces franchise elections, where group members vote to change who belongs to the electorate, in spatial ideological space. Shows using the Yolk social choice function that two-dimensional ideological space produces complex, cyclic disenfranchisement dynamics. Finds agents introducing a new ideological axis risk exclusion unless they ally with an existing side.

papers.title: Constrained Stochastic Policy Targeting under Heterogeneous Partial Interference
papers.abstract: Under heterogeneous interference, treating individuals with particular characteristics affects the population average outcome through their heterogeneous direct response to treatment and indirect effect on others, creating opportunities for efficient policy design. For instance, policymakers may minimize resource use by vaccinating individuals identified as superspreaders to achieve a target reduction in disease incidence. In such setting, we first study the problem of learning individualized stochastic treatment policies that minimize population average treatment probability subject to a prespecified outcome target. We propose an estimation approach based on a smooth surrogate for constraint violations and interference-aware inverse-probability-weighting or self-normalized estimators of the population average outcome, and establish finite-sample regret guarantees for both estimators. We also consider the complementary problem of maximizing the population average outcome subject to a constraint on average treatment probability. We apply the proposed methodology to a Colombian conditional cash transfer program aimed at improving school attendance. The application demonstrates that accounting for interference and individualizing treatment probabilities can reduce resource use relative to policies that ignore interference or impose homogeneous treatment probabilities.

papers.title: Making Experiment Results Comparable through Sitewide Impact Estimation
papers.abstract: Roblox spans many product surfaces-discovery, the virtual economy, creator tools-that differ sharply in reach and in how much the affected population contributes to any sitewide metric. A randomized experiment shows whether a treatment works for the users in its sample, but this experiment lift is not comparable across surfaces, because surfaces differ in reach and in their contribution to sitewide metrics. The quantity a strategic decision needs is a counterfactual-how much an aggregated sitewide metric (e.g., total platform play time) would move if the treatment reached 100% of its target population, which may be only part of the sitewide population, during the measurement period. We call this sitewide impact. Its scaling factor, which we call the coverage factor, combines the reach and the target population's contribution to the sitewide metric under no treatment. Hence a low-reach surface whose users carry much of the metric could outrank a high-reach surface whose users carry little. We develop two estimators under this framing: one for difference-in-means metrics and one for variant-level ratio metrics (a metric defined as a ratio of two population aggregates). Empirically, experiment lift is a poor proxy for sitewide impact-across 139 experiments that are statistically significant on time spent, the Spearman rank correlation between the two is 0.20, and 5 of the 10 largest experiment lifts are among the 10 largest sitewide impacts. We validate the estimator with A/A tests and against a long-term holdout, and apply it to cross-domain prioritization and attributing year-over-year growth to shipped innovations.
papers.topic_reason: Estimates aggregate platform-wide effects of experiments across population surfaces.
papers.one_sentence: Develops a sitewide impact estimator that scales experiment lift by a coverage factor combining reach and metric contribution. Introduces estimators for difference-in-means and ratio metrics, validated with A/A tests and a long-term holdout. Across 139 significant Roblox experiments, finds experiment lift and sitewide impact rank correlation of only 0.20.
papers.screen_reason: Measuring aggregate sitewide effects across product surfaces; scaling effects to population level.
